“Shalini ma'am, do you have five minutes?” Nirmala said, holding a printout, after the Monday meeting had emptied. Two colleagues lingered at the door, then left.
“Sure.”
“The vendor's deliveries have been late four times since January. I logged each one with the dates. I think we both want the March launch to hold, and this might help us plan.”
Shalini scanned the page. “In the meeting you said everything was fine.”
“I didn't want to raise it in front of everyone. I thought you would want to see it first.”
Shalini almost smiled. “Send me the log. I'll bring it up on Thursday. But the vendor contract renews in June, so don't expect fast change.”
“Understood. Thank you.”

qa.q: How many times had the vendor's deliveries been late since January?
qa.a: The vendor's deliveries had been late four times since January.

qa.q: Why did Nirmala say, “I didn't want to raise it in front of everyone”?
qa.a: Nirmala wanted to bring the problem in private and around the shared goal of the March launch, so that Shalini could take it in without feeling exposed.

qa.a: Nirmala could keep the log updated, share it again with Shalini and ask what support would help, accepting that change may be slow.

qa.a: Shalini may have been caught off guard but respected the private approach, since she almost smiled and offered to raise it on Thursday.

passage: I'm Kiran, and at twenty-four I was the newest analyst on a hospital's admin team. The night-shift roster had been overloaded for weeks, but in the Monday meeting the director praised everyone and the room stayed silent. Three colleagues studied their pens. I decided not to say it there. On Friday I went to Salma, the senior coordinator, with a two-week sheet of shifts and one sentence: “I think this is making handovers messy, and I'd like us to reach the same goal, safer handovers.” Salma read it twice. “Put it on one page for me,” she said. Not much changed for a month, and the director still snapped in meetings. But two shifts were swapped by spring, and I have learned to pick my moment.

qa.q: What did Kiran bring to Salma on Friday?
qa.a: Kiran brought a two-week sheet of shifts and one sentence.

qa.q: Why did Kiran decide not to speak in the Monday meeting?
qa.a: Kiran seems to have judged that a private, factual conversation would work better than speaking up in a silent room with the director present.

qa.a: Kiran could add another round of facts to Salma's one-page summary and ask what the next step could be, while accepting that some workplaces move slowly.

qa.q: How might Salma have seen Kiran's approach?
qa.a: Salma seems to have taken it seriously, since Salma read the sheet twice and asked for a one-page version to carry forward.

grounding: A young employee raises an issue with facts, in private and framed around the shared goal, and accepts that some cultures change slowly.

passage: The HR room at the agency smelled of coffee and toner. Payal placed her resignation letter on the desk. “Three months' notice, and I've written a handover plan for every client,” she said. Nilesh, the HR manager, glanced at it. “Is there anything that would make you stay?” Payal breathed out. “I have thought about it for weeks. I asked my head twice for changes in how juniors are spoken to and how numbers are reported. Nothing shifted, and I can't live inside that any more.” Through the glass, two people from her team pretended to sort files. The team head walked past without turning. “I'd like to leave properly,” Payal said. Nilesh nodded and slid a pen across.

qa.q: How much notice did Payal offer?
qa.a: Payal offered three months' notice.

qa.q: What is Payal feeling when Payal says, “I can't live inside that any more”?
qa.a: Payal is settled but weary after weeks of thought: the workplace's ways are ones that Payal cannot accept, and the calm handover plan shows a wish to leave with dignity.

qa.a: They may have felt unsettled, torn between curiosity and worry about their own place, which fits pretending to sort files instead of looking away.

passage:
Subject: Decision
Dear Jyoti,
Thank you for the coffee last Sunday. You asked whether I was sure, so here is my honest reasoning. For eight months I have watched the team praise whoever shouts loudest and quietly blame whoever isn't in the room. At first I told myself to adapt. Last week I caught myself rehearsing the same lines, and I didn't like the sound of them. I have listed what I can control: I'll finish the current project properly, give clear notice in April, update my portfolio and speak to two people in the industry whom I trust. I'll also thank the colleagues who were kind. Staying and shrinking would cost me more slowly than leaving. I would like to leave with my name intact.
Pankaj

qa.q: Until which month will Pankaj give notice?
qa.a: Pankaj plans to give clear notice in April.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj say, “I didn't like the sound of them”?
qa.a: Pankaj was alarmed to hear the workplace's habits in Pankaj's own voice, which suggests shrinking to fit had already started.

qa.a: Pankaj will finish the project, give clear notice in April, update the portfolio, speak to two trusted people in the industry and thank the kind colleagues.

qa.a: Jyoti may feel reassured that the decision is careful and not rushed, since the email lays out reasons and a plan.

Counsellor's note, Friday. Our school lost a Class 9 student, Neha, suddenly on Tuesday. Today the whole school gathered in the hall. I watched the students carefully. Some cried openly. Some laughed nervously in the corridor and then went white. Alka, in Class 9, joked with friends all morning, then sat alone by the water tank for a long time. Several did not speak at all. I told the groups that there is no wrong way to feel and no right one. Students who wanted to could come to my room in small groups, and their parents were informed today. I spoke to Alka individually and will call home this afternoon to arrange more support.
Disha, school counsellor

Pallavi's diary, Wednesday night.
The whole school was silent in assembly today because of Neha. Some girls cried so hard they had to be taken out. Jomon kept cracking jokes in the corridor afterwards, and I got so angry that I told him to stop. He looked at me strangely and walked away. Later I saw him sitting on the back steps, not saying anything. I felt terrible. I don't think the jokes mean he doesn't care. passage: “Sit, child, sit. When my father died I was twenty-six, and the three of us grieved so differently that we nearly broke as a family. On the eleventh night Parveen stopped in the doorway with a file in his hand and said, ‘I don't know how to sit.’ We all laughed and cried at once. That night we finally sat together.”

qa.a: They could have asked each other how each was coping, and understood that quiet, talking and busy work were all ways of grieving.

qa.a: They could take turns, with a little time for papers and a little for the photographs and silence, so each style of grieving has room.

qa.q: How might Chinmay have felt when Chinmay put down the files?
qa.a: Chinmay may have felt a mixture of shame and relief at seeing Aparna's grief, and realised the papers could wait a little.

grounding: A family member grieves quietly while another talks and another keeps busy with tasks, each thinking the others are not grieving properly.
